newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans seeking 9-millimetre solution to crime.
newsitem.headline: S.Africans seeking 9-millimetre solution to crime.

text.p: You get home from work and find two men running out the door with the colour TV set. Do you blow them away?
"Damn right," say some South Africans. "Dead wrong," say the police.

Alarmed by Johannesburg's high crime rate, more people are applying for licenses to own the Brownings, Smith and Wessons, Colts, Glocks, Sig-Sauers, CZs and other 9-millimetre or larger calibre automatics on sale in the city's many gunshops.
But, police say public ignorance about the legal use of handguns is itself alarming.

Undermanned and short of funds, they do not have the resources to undertake a nationwide firearms testing system. In the Fairlands suburb of Johannesburg, however, police have devised their own test to detect trigger-happy, Charlie Bronson style vigilantes.
It takes the form of an three-page, 11-part questionnaire designed to probe a person's willingness to open fire.

"We are seeing a substantial increase in (gun licence) applications. But many people do not seem to know the law regarding the circumstances in which they may use a firearm," Superintendent Jaco Oosthuysen of Fairlands told Reuters.
He said the question came up often at community-police forums, where people were evidently unclear about the law.
"It seems that people are very tensed up and scared. We get the perception that many want to shoot to kill, especially if they've been robbed and don't intend to let it happen again.

"But legal firearms are for self-defence when your own life or the lives of others are threatened, not for gunning down the thief who stole your handbag. And if you must shoot, the intention should be to wound, unless your life's at risk."
The questionnaire offers a somewhat startling insight into life in South Africa's crime capital. Here's a sample:
"You are sitting on your patio when someone jumps over the wall and this person has some object in his hand. What would you do if you had a firearm?"

It goes on to ask: Would you shoot someone who puts a knife to your throat and grabs your briefcase in the street? Would you open fire on four men stealing a car, or shoot two men raping a woman, or gun down someone outside your house who has broken a window?
What about the shop-owner who shouts that the man who has just run past you has stolen a soft drink. Do you shoot?

Senior superintendent Andrew Lesch, spokesman for the police's national support services, said police were trying their best to ensure gun-owners had adequate knowledge of the law. This would protect the public and gun-owners against misuse of firearms with serious legal consequences.

"It is indeed alarming how very aggressive some of them are, especially victims of crime," he said. "They just seem to want to blow the lights out of them (criminals), without realising the potentially negative consequences," Lesch said.

At the same time, he said, many people owned firearms for years without even bothering with regular practice sessions, raising the question whether they would know what to do with a gun if ever they faced a life-threatening situation.
Oosthuysen said his station sergeant, Braam Peens, devised the questionnaire to single out those in clear need of some "schooling" on the law, as well as mandatory practical training.
South African gun law was clear enough, he said, but he knew of no simple, illustrated handbook that would spell out for the uninitiated when and when not they could lawfully use a gun.
"With the questionnaire, we can test their knowledge and see if there's some wrong impression to be corrected."
Oosthuysen said many of the applicants, who answer the questions on the spot, give wrong answers.
"For example, we ask what they'd do if they're robbed on a downtown street and lots say: 'I'll shoot him.' We must explain to them, that's impossible. Think of all the bystanders."
